entry: English actor best known for playing [[Harry Potter]] in all eight films of the series, from 2001 to 2011. He began stage acting in 2007 in *Equus* and later earned a Tony Award for Best Featured Actor in a Musical for *Merrily We Roll Along* (2023). His leading film roles have grossed over $8.38 billion worldwide. Other films include *The Woman in Black* (2012) and *The Lost City* (2022).

Protagonist of the *Book of Daniel* in the [[Hebrew Bible]]. In that account, Daniel was a noble Jewish youth of [[Jerusalem]] taken into captivity by [[Nebuchadnezzar II]] of [[Babylon]], who served the king and his successors until the time of the Persian conqueror [[Cyrus the Great|Cyrus]]. Most scholars agree that Daniel, as depicted in the book, was not a historical figure, and that the character was probably based on a legendary Daniel from earlier traditions. Some conservative scholars hold that he existed and that the book was written in the 6th century BCE. Six cities claim his tomb, the most famous at [[Susa]] in southern Iran. He is not a prophet in [[Judaism]], but rabbinic tradition regarded him as the most distinguished member of the Babylonian diaspora. Christianity considers him a prophet, and although he is not mentioned in the [[Quran]], Muslim sources describe him as one.

Prince of Galicia and Volhynia, and king of Ruthenia (1253–1266). Son of Roman Mstislavich of Volhynia. Under his long rule the Romanovichi branch of the [[Rurikids]] restored control over [[Galicia (Eastern Europe)|Galicia]], and the reunited principality rose to become a prominent power, eventually elevated to the status of a kingdom. He withstood the Mongol invasions, making him a defining figure in the later period of [[Kievan Rus']] after the decline of [[Kyiv|Kiev]], and he was grand prince of Kiev in 1240. The *Galician-Volhynian Chronicle* praised him as an exemplary ruler, brave warrior and wise statesman, whose qualities made him second only to [[Solomon]].

Sovereign state, officially the Kingdom of Denmark, comprising metropolitan Denmark and two autonomous regions, the [[Faroe Islands]] and [[Greenland]]. The Faroe Islands and Greenland have been under the Crown of Denmark since 1397 (de facto) and part of the realm since 1814 (de jure). They were granted home rule in 1946 and 1979, respectively, and in 2009 Greenland received "self rule." The kingdom is a unitary sovereign state, not a federation, with legislative, executive and judicial powers exercised for the whole realm.

North Germanic language of the Indo-European family, spoken mainly in Denmark. About 5.5 million people speak it, with communities in [[Greenland]], the [[Faroe Islands]], [[Iceland]] and southern Schleswig in [[Germany]], where it has minority-language status. Danish descends from Old Norse, like Swedish, from the East Norse dialect group. Until the 16th century it was a continuum of dialects; after the [[Reformation|Protestant Reformation]] and the printing press, a standard language developed on the dialect of [[Copenhagen]]. A nationalist movement later adopted it as a token of Danish identity, and 18th- and 19th-century literature enlarged its use. Danish has 27 phonemically distinctive [[Vowel|vowels]] and the prosodic feature *stød*, a kind of laryngeal phonation. Its word order is V2.

English film director and producer. His debut film, *Shallow Grave* (1994), earned the BAFTA Award for Best British Film. *Slumdog Millionaire* (2008) earned him the Academy Award, BAFTA Award and Golden Globe Award for Best Director. Other films include *Trainspotting* (1996), *28 Days Later* (2002), *Sunshine* (2007), *127 Hours* (2010), *Steve Jobs* (2015) and *Yesterday* (2019). He was artistic director of the opening ceremony of the 2012 Summer Olympics in [[London]], which received wide praise.

American film composer and songwriter. He was lead vocalist and principal songwriter for the new wave band Oingo Boingo in the early 1980s. Since scoring his first studio film in 1985, he has composed over 100 feature film scores. He has frequently worked with director [[Tim Burton]], contributing music to nearly 20 of his projects, including *Batman*, *Edward Scissorhands* and *Big Fish*. His other scores include *Spider-Man*, the *Men in Black* films and the themes for *Desperate Housewives* and *The Simpsons*. His honors include four Oscar nominations, three Emmy Awards and a Grammy.

Second-longest river in Europe, after the Volga. It flows southeast from the [[Black Forest]] of Germany through Central and Southeastern Europe to the [[Black Sea]], passing through the Danube Delta in Romania. Once a frontier of the [[Roman Empire]], it connects ten European countries. Four national capitals lie on its banks: [[Vienna]], [[Bratislava]], [[Budapest]] and [[Belgrade]]. Its drainage basin of 817,000 sq km (315,000 sq mi) extends into nine more countries. About 2,415 km (1,501 mi) of the river is navigable, and the Rhine–Main–Danube Canal links it to the North Sea. The river is also an important source of [[Hydropower|hydropower]] and drinking water.

Largest city and financial hub of Tanzania, on the [[Swahili]] coast. Its name, commonly translated from Arabic as "abode of peace," was given when Sultan Majid bin Said of [[Zanzibar]] began building the city in 1865 or 1866. It became the main administrative and commercial center of German East Africa. After World War II it grew rapidly, and the 1967 ujamaa policy made Tanzania lean towards [[Socialism|socialism]]. A 1974 decision to move the capital to Dodoma was completed in 1996, but the city still hosts most government offices. With a population of over 7 million, it is the largest city in [[East Africa]] and the fifth-largest in Africa.

Narrow strait in northwestern [[Turkey]], connecting the [[Aegean Sea]] with the Sea of Marmara. Also called the Strait of Gallipoli and, in classical antiquity, the Hellespont, it forms part of the continental boundary between Asia and Europe. Together with the [[Bosporus]], it forms the Turkish Straits. One of the world's narrowest straits used for international navigation, it is 61 km (38 mi) long and 1.2 to 6 km (0.75 to 3.73 mi) wide, with an average depth of 55 m (180 ft). Control of the strait has long been contested, including in the [[Peloponnesian War]], the [[Gallipoli campaign|Gallipoli Campaign]] of World War I and the [[Turkish War of Independence]]. Under the 1936 Montreux Convention, civilian vessels have peacetime freedom of passage.

Remote, roadless rainforest area on the border between [[Colombia]] and [[Panama]]. It is the only land bridge between [[North America]] and [[South America]], and it has long served as a route for humans and wildlife. Its terrain is difficult, and law enforcement and medical support are nonexistent. The [[Pan-American Highway]] is interrupted here, breaking at Yaviza, Panama, and resuming at Turbo, Colombia, about 106 km (66 mi) away. Since the 2010s, hundreds of thousands of migrants, primarily Haitians and Venezuelans, have crossed the Gap northward; more than 520,000 individuals passed through it in 2023.

Persian king of the [[Achaemenid Empire]] (r. 522–486 BCE). He came to the throne after overthrowing the king Bardiya (or Smerdis), whom he claimed was an impostor named Gaumata, and he quelled the rebellions that followed. At its territorial peak the empire included much of West Asia, parts of the Balkans and the Caucasus, Central Asia, the Indus Valley and [[Egypt]]. He divided it into provinces governed by satraps, introduced a uniform monetary system, made [[Aramaic]] a co-official language beside Old Persian, improved roads and standardized weights and measures. Construction projects centered on [[Susa]], [[Persepolis]] and [[Babylon]]. A trilingual inscription at Mount Behistun, recording his conquests, became a key source for the decipherment of [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]]. Greek sources describe his punitive expedition against [[Athens]] for its role in the Ionian Revolt.

City in northern [[West Bengal]], India, in the Eastern Himalayas, at an average elevation of 2,045 m (6,709 ft). [[Kangchenjunga]], the world's third-highest mountain, rises to the north. During [[East India Company]] rule in the early 19th century, British officials identified the site as a summer retreat. Laborers recruited chiefly from [[Nepal]] cleared forest for [[Tea|tea]] plantations, and tea and tourism remain the mainstays of the economy. The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway, a narrow-gauge line built in the late 19th century, was declared a World Heritage Site by [[UNESCO]] in 1999.

Proposed form of energy driving the accelerated expansion of the [[Universe|universe]]. It also slows the rate of structure formation. In the lambda-CDM model, dark energy makes up about 68% of the total mass-energy of the present-day observable universe, compared with 27% for [[Dark matter|dark matter]] and 5% for ordinary matter. Its density is very low, about 7×10⁻³⁰ g/cm³, but because it is uniform across space it dominates the universe's mass-energy. Evidence first came from measurements of [[Supernova|Type Ia supernovae]], whose constant luminosity allows accurate distance measurement; their redshift showed that expansion is accelerating. The simplest explanation is the [[Cosmological constant]], first proposed by Einstein, although scalar fields such as quintessence are also considered. Its nature remains unknown.

[[Comedy]] that makes light of [[Taboo|taboo]] subjects, also known as black comedy. Also called black humor, gallows humor or morbid humor, it aims to provoke discomfort, serious thought and uncomfortable amusement. Unlike blue comedy, which focuses on nudity, sex and body fluids, dark humor treats serious subjects, especially death. The French term *humour noir* was coined by Surrealist theorist André Breton, who in his 1940 *Anthology of Black Humor* credited [[Jonathan Swift]] as its originator. Literary critics have associated the genre with [[Aristophanes]] in ancient Greece. Saint Lawrence, patron saint of comedians, made a dark joke while being burned to death on a rotisserie.

Invisible, hypothetical form of matter that does not interact with electromagnetic radiation, including light. Its existence is inferred from gravitational effects that general relativity cannot explain unless more matter is present than is observed, such as in the motion of [[Galaxy|galaxies]] and in [[Cosmic microwave background|cosmic microwave background]] anisotropies. In the standard lambda-CDM model, dark matter makes up 26.8% of the mass-energy of the universe, against 5% for ordinary matter and 68.2% for [[Dark energy|dark energy]]. It is thought to provide gravitational scaffolding for cosmic structures. The leading candidates are unknown particles such as weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) or axions; the main alternative is [[Black hole|primordial black holes]]. Most astrophysicists accept its existence, though a minority argue for modified gravity theories such as MOND, and none of these explains all observations.

Type of interstellar cloud, particularly a [[Molecular cloud|molecular cloud]], dense enough to obscure visible light. Also called an absorption nebula, it blocks the light of background stars and of emission or reflection nebulae. Dust grains coated with frozen [[Carbon monoxide|carbon monoxide]] and nitrogen cause the extinction in the coldest, densest parts of molecular clouds. Dark nebulae form part of molecular cloud complexes, and isolated small ones are called Bok globules. The largest nearby dark nebulae are visible to the naked eye as dark patches against the [[Milky Way]], such as the Coalsack Nebula and the Great Rift. [[Star formation|Star formation]] and maser emission take place in their central regions.

World Wide Web content that exists on darknets, which are overlay networks on the [[Internet]] requiring specific software, configurations or authorization to access. Darknets such as [[Tor (network)|Tor]], I2P and Hyphanet let users communicate anonymously, because traffic passes through many intermediate servers under layers of [[Encryption|encryption]]. The dark web forms a small part of the [[Deep web|deep web]], the part of the Web not indexed by [[Search engine|search engines]], although the two terms are often confused. Tor sites use the .onion domain.

Family of mainly tropical waterbirds (Anhingidae), also called anhingas or snakebirds. The family contains a single genus, *Anhinga*, with four living species in the Americas, Africa, Asia and Australasia. The name snakebird refers to the long, thin neck, which looks like a snake when the bird swims with its body submerged. The name darter alludes to the way they impale fish with their thin, pointed bills. The American darter, *A. anhinga*, is also called the anhinga or water turkey in the southern United States. Darters are large birds, and males have darker plumage and a larger bill than females. They inhabit freshwater lakes, rivers, marshes and swamps, often in flocks that associate with [[Stork|storks]], [[Heron|herons]] and [[Ibis|ibises]]. On dry land they walk with a high-stepped gait, wings spread for balance, as [[Pelican|pelicans]] do. They feed mainly on mid-sized [[Fish|fish]] and are highly territorial on the nest.

Fictional Sith Lord and major villain of the [[Star Wars]] franchise. A former Jedi Knight, Anakin Skywalker, he is lured to the dark side of the Force by Chancellor Palpatine. Severely injured in a lightsaber duel with Obi-Wan Kenobi, he is transformed into a [[Cyborg|cyborg]] and serves Palpatine for over two decades. Vader turns against Palpatine and kills him when Palpatine tries to kill Vader's son, Luke Skywalker. David Prowse physically portrayed him in the original trilogy, and [[James Earl Jones]] provided his voice in all of the films.

Private [[Ivy League]] research university in Hanover, New Hampshire. Founded in 1769 by Eleazar Wheelock and Samson Occom to train Native American Christian missionaries, it is one of the nine colonial colleges chartered before the [[American Revolution]]. Its student enrollment of about 6,700 makes it the smallest university in the Ivy League. The acceptance rate was 5.3% for the class of 2028. The university operates on a quarter system, and its alumni include 170 members of the [[United States Congress]] and three [[Nobel Prize]] laureates.

Competitive sport and pub game in which players throw small, sharp-pointed darts at a round target called a dartboard. Points are scored by hitting marked areas spread across the board, unlike in [[Archery|archery]], where points rise toward the center. The game is commonly played in the [[British Isles]] and enjoyed around the world. In 1908 darts was declared a game of skill, allowing it in pubs, after a Leeds landlord was prosecuted for playing it on licensed premises. Before [[World War I]], dartboards were made of elm, which was easily damaged. From 1935 they were made of compressed sisal fibers bound with a metal ring, a more durable design.

Capital and largest city of the [[Northern Territory]], Australia. With 139,902 residents at the 2021 census, it holds nearly 63% of the territory's population and is the smallest, wettest and most northerly of Australia's capital cities. Darwin is a link to [[Southeast Asia]], including Indonesia and [[Timor-Leste]]. The Larrakia people are its traditional owners. John Clements Wickham named the region Port Darwin in honor of [[Charles Darwin]]. The settlement was renamed Darwin in 1911. The city has been almost entirely rebuilt four times, after cyclones in 1897 and 1937, Japanese air raids in World War II, and Cyclone Tracy in 1974.

Three-volume work of political economy by [[Karl Marx]], foundational to Marxist theory. Its full title is *Capital: A Critique of Political Economy*. Only the first volume appeared in Marx's lifetime, in 1867; [[Friedrich Engels]] published the second and third from Marx's manuscripts in 1885 and 1894. Its central argument is that capitalism depends on the exploitation of labor, whose unpaid work is the source of surplus value and [[Profit (economics)|profit]]. Marx held a labor theory of value and argued that the rate of profit tends to fall, leading to economic crises. Volume I covers production, Volume II the circulation of [[Capital (economics)|capital]], and Volume III the distribution of surplus value into profit, [[Interest (economics)|interest]] and rent. The work drew on [[Adam Smith]], [[David Ricardo]] and [[Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel|Hegel]]. Its association with 20th-century communist states has made it a subject of continuing debate.

Ten principal [[Avatar|avatars]] of the Hindu god [[Vishnu]], who is said to descend in these forms to restore cosmic order ([[Dharma|dharma]]). The most accepted list, found in the Puranas, names Matsya, Kurma, Varaha, Narasimha, Vamana, Parashurama, Rama, [[Krishna]] and [[The Buddha|Buddha]] as the eighth and ninth, though some traditions substitute Balarama for Krishna. All have appeared except [[Kalki]], who will come at the end of the [[Kali Yuga]]. Versions vary by region and sect.
